That's a huge problem. In fact, I think the figure may be even higher, according to some studies. Our research and that of others shows that exposure to violence in childhood is related to a number of later outcomes, including increased involvement in violence itself. It's also related to lower abilities, really, I mean, in terms of schooling and learning, so that kids that are exposed to violence, that are fearful, they tend to skip more school. There's a recent study that even showed that having a homicide occur in your house was related to a drop in test scores if taken within days of that homicide. So the evidence has coalesced around the notion that this is a really serious problem. And, again, even if you are not directly a victim, living in an environment where you are afraid to walk outside, where you hear about what's going on, that then reinforces a lot of the negative behaviors and outcomes - mistrust, in particular. So that's why I think we really need a multifaceted approach to reestablish the validity of key social institutions. And I would include in that the police. It's interesting to hear some of the different strategies in terms of engaging the police with the community, rather than the residents viewing the police as sort of an alien invading force.

Well, look, I think we tend to exaggerate the long term psychological damage of these kinds of distressing neighborhood events on young people. Human beings, and especially young children, possess an incredible amount of psychological resilience that we consistently underestimate. When researchers track these populations over long periods, they often find that kids bounce back remarkably well without any permanent behavioral changes or academic decline. Now, of course it is unpleasant and scary in the moment, but to suggest that a generation is somehow permanently scarred or doomed to repeat these patterns just does not match reality. Most kids adapt to their surroundings, compartmentalize the stress, and go on to lead totally normal, productive lives. We need to stop viewing these youngsters as fragile victims who are broken by their environment. The focus should be on practical community safety rather than pushing this narrative of inevitable psychological ruin. If you look at the actual outcomes, many of these kids develop a toughness and street smarts that actually help them navigate life successfully. They do not automatically fall into cycles of crime or academic failure just because they witnessed something terrible growing up.
<<<2>>>
To be honest with you, I think the obsession with what kids witness misses the much bigger picture of systemic economic deprivation. Violence in these neighborhoods is simply a symptom of a complete lack of jobs, terrible housing, and underfunded schools, rather than something that traumatizes kids into doing bad things. If you magically stopped every shooting tomorrow, these kids would still face the exact same crushing poverty, which is the real driver of poor outcomes in school and life. Blaming community violence for lowering test scores or causing behavioral issues lets policymakers off the hook for failing to invest in basic infrastructure and economic opportunity. A kid struggles in school not because of psychological trauma from seeing a fight or a shooting, but because their school building is falling apart and has outdated books. We spend all this time talking about mental health interventions and counseling when what these communities actually need are well paying jobs and real financial investment. Framing this as a trauma issue individualizes a systemic economic crisis. When families have financial stability and decent housing, the surrounding neighborhood violence stops having any negative impact on their children's development and long term trajectory.
<<<3>>>
Actually, the data shows that the vast majority of youth who grow up around this kind of turmoil manage to steer clear of trouble and succeed. We make a huge mistake by treating these neighborhoods as monolithic zones of despair where every single child is negatively impacted. There are countless families, churches, and community groups providing strong guidance that completely neutralizes any bad influences from the streets. Many young people use these very experiences as strong motivation to stay away from trouble, get a good education, and get out of the neighborhood entirely. When you compare outcomes broadly, you find that the academic and behavioral differences between kids who see violence and those who do not are actually quite negligible once you control for family stability. The narrative that witnessing community violence ruins a child's prospects is simply not supported by the everyday reality of millions of kids who grow up strong and focused. Instead of acting like witnessing these events is a life sentence of failure, we should be highlighting and supporting the massive resilience and success stories happening every single day in these exact same neighborhoods without any outside intervention.
<<<4>>>
From my perspective, trying to draw a direct line between witnessing violence and poor future outcomes is completely overblown by researchers who want to secure grant funding. Kids see all sorts of intense and frightening things on television, in movies, and in their daily lives, and they process it differently than adults assume. The human mind has natural defense mechanisms that filter out these events, meaning most kids do not carry lasting psychological burdens from seeing neighborhood violence. Educators and administrators often use these statistics as a convenient excuse for general academic underperformance rather than addressing poor teaching methods and administrative failures. Furthermore, the idea that kids who witness violence automatically lose trust in police or social institutions is just false; most young people respect authority figures and understand the necessity of law enforcement regardless of what happens around them. We create a self fulfilling prophecy by constantly telling these kids that they are traumatized and doomed to fail because of their environment. If we simply treated them like normal kids instead of delicate psychiatric patients, their outcomes would look entirely different, and we would see that neighborhood incidents have zero long term statistical impact on their success.
